prompt:
You map a 0–1 knob value to a filter cutoff from 20 Hz to 20 kHz with this exponential map:

```formula
f = f_lo (f_hi / f_lo)^x
where
f: the cutoff frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_lo: the cutoff at x = 0, here 20 Hz
f_hi: the cutoff at x = 1, here 20 kHz
x: the knob value, from 0 to 1, no unit
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: each step of the knob multiplies the frequency by the same ratio, so the 1,000:1 range is spread evenly in pitch.
```

In code that is `f = 20 * 1000**x`. What cutoff do you get with the knob at the middle (normalised position 0.5)?

options.explanation: That is the *linear* mapping 20 + 0.5 × 19,980. The formula given is exponential.
Correct. 1,000 to the power 0.5 is the square root of 1,000, about 31.62, and 20 Hz × 31.62 ≈ 632 Hz: the geometric midpoint of 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
Close to the right region, but not what the formula gives: 20 Hz times the square root of 1,000 is about 632 Hz.
This assumes the midpoint of the range is halfway in hertz, which is the linear assumption the exponential mapping avoids.

workedExample:
Substitute x = 0.5. A power of 0.5 is a square root:

```formula
f = f_lo (f_hi / f_lo)^x
f = 20 Hz × (20000 / 20)^0.5
f = 20 Hz × 1000^0.5
f ≈ 20 Hz × 31.62 ≈ 632.5 Hz
where
f: the cutoff frequency, in hertz (Hz)
f_lo: the bottom of the range, 20 Hz
f_hi: the top of the range, 20 kHz
x: the knob value, here 0.5
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
≈: approximately equal to
In words: halfway along the knob is 31.6 times the bottom frequency.
```

Check: 632 / 20 ≈ 31.6 and 20,000 / 632 ≈ 31.6. Equal ratios on each side, so it is the midpoint in logarithmic frequency. The perceived cutoff sweep still depends on the filter and signal.

link.title: Introduction to Digital Filters — J. O. Smith, CCRMA

prompt: Which parameters are usually better mapped exponentially (or in decibels) than linearly from a knob? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Pitch perception is logarithmic: an octave is a doubling wherever you are on the scale.
Correct. Useful times span milliseconds to seconds; an exponential map gives fine control at the short end.
Pan is usually mapped linearly in position (with a pan law applied to gains), not exponentially across the knob.

Correct. A dB-based map gives equal amplitude ratios per knob step and useful control over a wide level range. Equal perceived loudness steps are not guaranteed across signals or listening conditions.

workedExample:
Choose the parameter scale and usable range, rather than assuming one universal perceptual law.

| Parameter | Judged by |
|---|---|
| Frequency | Ratio |
| Envelope time | Often a wide ratio range |
| Gain | Equal ratios in dB |
| Pan | Position |

Exponential maps provide equal ratios and often useful fine control at the lower end; test the selected parameter and sound.
